questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: simplify the difference quotient for a power function
questions.stem: The difference quotient for the function f of x equal to x squared, evaluated at the point where x equals 3, is the fraction whose numerator is x squared minus 9 and whose denominator is x minus 3. What does it simplify to?

options.text: x + 3, which comes from factoring x squared - 9 as (x - 3)(x + 3)
x - 3, which comes from dropping the 9 from the numerator
options.misconception: keeps only the denominator's factor and loses the other one

options.text: 3x, which comes from multiplying the two x-values instead of subtracting
options.misconception: replaces the difference of the two x-values with their product

options.text: 9, which is just the value the function takes at the point x = 3
options.misconception: confuses the limit of the quotient with the function value at 3

questions.explanation: The numerator is a difference of two squares, so x squared minus 9 factors as (x - 3)(x + 3), and the (x - 3) then cancels with the denominator, leaving x + 3. That cancellation is valid for every x except 3, and the limit as x approaches 3 is 3 + 3 = 6, which is the derivative. The cancellation is the whole reason the difference quotient can be evaluated at all, since the quotient is undefined exactly at the point being studied.
questions.hint: Look for a difference of two squares in the numerator, then cancel against the denominator.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: explain why the sine derivative comes from a standard limit
questions.stem: Why does the derivative of the sine function have to be built from a limit argument rather than from the usual power-rule factoring?

options.text: the numerator of the difference quotient is a difference of trig values, which no algebraic factorisation touches, so a standard trig limit is needed
sine is not a polynomial, so no differentiation rule applies to it at all
options.misconception: concludes that a non-polynomial function has no derivative

options.text: sine stays between minus 1 and 1, so its rate of change must be zero
options.misconception: treats a bounded function as one that cannot change at all

options.text: sine is periodic, so no single rate of change can be defined anywhere
options.misconception: believes a repeating graph rules out a local rate of change

questions.explanation: Every elementary derivative starts as a limit of a difference quotient, and for sine the numerator is the difference of two sine values rather than a difference of powers, so the factorisation that rescues the power function is unavailable. The limit is instead evaluated with the angle-addition identity, which writes the difference of sines as a product and reduces the ratio to the single standard limit that the limit of sine t over t equals 1, and the factor that survives is the cosine. Boundedness and periodicity are irrelevant here, since the cosine is itself bounded and varies.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the numerator of the difference quotient for a trig function.

questions.learningObjective: state the derivatives of the exponential and natural logarithm
questions.stem: Which pairing of derivatives is correct for the natural exponential function and the natural logarithm?

options.text: the derivative of e to the x is e to the x itself, and the derivative of ln of x is 1 over x
the derivative of e to the x is 1, and the derivative of ln of x is e to the x

options.text: the derivative of e to the x is e to the x over x, and the derivative of ln of x is x
options.misconception: divides the exponential by its input and inverts the logarithm's rule

questions.explanation: The natural exponential is its own derivative, which is unusual and worth memorising as a fact, while the natural logarithm differentiates to the reciprocal of its input. The two are inverses of each other, and the chain rule ties the pair together: since the log of e to the x is x, differentiating that identity forces the two rules to be reciprocal to one another. Option C's expression for the exponential is the familiar power rule with a minus 1 glued on, which belongs to no standard function here.
questions.hint: One of these two functions is its own derivative; the other is the reciprocal of its input.

questions.learningObjective: state the chain rule for a composite function
questions.stem: The function g of x equal to the sine of x squared is a composite of an inner function x squared and an outer function sine. What does the chain rule say its derivative is?

the derivative of the outer function, plus the derivative of the inner function
options.misconception: adds the two rates instead of multiplying them

options.text: the derivative of the inner function, raised to the outer function's power
options.misconception: reuses a power-rule shape on a function that is not a power

options.text: the derivatives of both functions, with the outer one divided by the inner one
options.misconception: divides the two rates rather than multiplying them

questions.explanation: A small change in the final output is caused by a small change in the inner value, and the inner value changes at its own rate, so the two rates multiply rather than add. For the example, that is 2x times the cosine of x squared. The multiplication is what makes the rule composable: a function buried three layers deep contributes a factor at each layer, and the factors are all evaluated and multiplied in one product.
questions.hint: Rates of change along a chain of two links multiply; they do not add.

questions.learningObjective: explain why implicit differentiation is sometimes necessary

an implicit curve has no derivative that can be found by any method at all

options.misconception: blames the algebra of the square root rather than the lack of a function

options.text: a derivative can be formed only when y is written before x in the relation

The only thing the method requires is the chain rule, since y itself depends on x, and that is the factor of 2y. The failure is not about square roots or notation; it is that near the top the curve is not the graph of any single function of x.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: differentiate a power function and check it against the definition
questions.stem: A rate of change is needed at the point where x equals 2 for the function f of x equal to x to the fourth power. What is the value of f prime there?
questions.explanation: The power rule gives 4x cubed, and at x = 2 that is 4 times 8 = 32. The definition agrees: the difference quotient is ((2 + h) to the fourth minus 16) over h, and expanding by the binomial formula gives 32 + 24h + 8h squared + h cubed, whose limit as h shrinks to 0 is 32. A sign error in the expansion would shift the result, and 24h is the term that vanishes, not the whole expression.
questions.hint: Apply the power rule, then confirm with the difference quotient at a small step size.

questions.learningObjective: differentiate a polynomial and check it against the difference quotient
questions.stem: The function f of x equals 3x squared minus 5x plus 2. What is the value of f prime at the point where x equals 4?
questions.explanation: Differentiating term by term gives 6x minus 5, and at x = 4 that is 24 - 5 = 19. The difference quotient confirms it and shows exactly why: the value at 4 plus h minus the value at 4 works out to 3(8h + h squared) - 5h all over h, which is 19 + 3h, and the h term vanishes. The constant 2 never contributes, since its difference is zero, which is why it is absent from the derivative.
questions.hint: Differentiate each term, then verify with a small step size in the definition.

questions.stem: Let f of x equal the quantity 2x plus 3 raised to the fourth power. What is the value of f prime at the point where x equals 1?

The check that needs no chain rule at all is to expand first: (2x + 3) to the fourth is 16x to the fourth plus 96x cubed plus 216x squared plus 216x plus 81, whose derivative at 1 is 64 + 288 + 432 + 216, again 1000. Forgetting the inner factor of 2 would give 500, exactly half.
questions.hint: Multiply the outer derivative by the derivative of the bracket, then substitute.

questions.stem: The function f of x equals 3 sine of x plus 4 cosine of x. What is the value of f prime at the point where x equals pi over 2?

Both signs matter: the sine term becomes a cosine and keeps its coefficient, while the cosine term becomes a negative sine, and losing that minus sign would give 4 instead. A numerical difference quotient at that point returns the same -4.

questions.stem: Let f of x equal x times the natural logarithm of x. What is the value of f prime at the point where x equals 2? Give the answer to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The product rule gives the natural logarithm of x plus x times 1 over x, and the second term is exactly 1, so the derivative is ln x + 1, which at x = 2 is 1.693 to three decimal places. The cancellation of x with 1 over x is worth watching, since dropping it would give ln 2 alone, about 0.693. A numerical difference quotient centred at 2 returns 1.693147, matching the closed form.

The linear and constant terms of the original polynomial drop out at the first differentiation, which is why the answer depends only on the quadratic and quartic parts. A numerical second difference quotient taken at 2 returns 42.0 as well, confirming the algebra.

options.misconception: reports the magnitude of the linear term and drops the quadratic one

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: compute the price elasticity of demand from a demand function
questions.stem: A product's demand function is p equal to 40 minus one half of q, where p is the price in dollars and q the quantity demanded. What is the price elasticity of demand at the point where q equals 20?

options.text: about 0.33
about 0.67
options.misconception: forgets to divide the price change by the price level itself

options.text: about 1.50
options.misconception: reports the ratio of quantity to slope without inverting it

options.text: about 30.00
options.misconception: uses the price level alone and drops the rate of change

questions.explanation: Elasticity is the percentage change in quantity divided by the percentage change in price, which in calculus notation is the magnitude of the price derivative times quantity over price. At q = 20 the price is 40 - 10 = 30 and the slope is minus one half, so the elasticity is 0.5 times 20 over 30, which is one third, about 0.33. Reading it in words, a 1 percent rise in price costs about 0.33 percent of demand, so demand is inelastic there and a price rise would raise revenue.
questions.hint: Multiply the rate of price change by quantity and divide by the price level.

questions.learningObjective: handle the inconclusive case of the second derivative test
questions.stem: A student checks the function f of x equal to x to the fourth power at x equals 0, finds that f prime of 0 and f double prime of 0 are both 0, and concludes that x equals 0 is a local maximum. What is correct?

the test is inconclusive, and only a long numerical search can classify the point
options.misconception: believes an inconclusive test cannot be resolved by other means

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: explain the need for implicit differentiation on a circle
questions.stem: Explain why the circle x squared plus y squared equals 25 needs implicit differentiation near its topmost point, and what the method delivers there.

answer.exemplar: Near the top of the circle the relation x squared + y squared = 25 fails the vertical line test, because the line x = 0 meets the circle in the single point (0, 5) while nearby vertical lines meet it in two points with the same y, and any attempt to write y as a function of x has to choose one of them and discard the other. So the difficulty is not algebraic but structural: there is no single function there to differentiate. Implicit differentiation sidesteps it. Differentiate both sides with respect to x while treating y as a function of x, and the chain rule contributes a factor of the derivative of y with respect to x, giving 2x + 2y times that derivative equals 0, and hence the slope is minus x over y. At the topmost point (0, 5) that gives a slope of 0, which is exactly right since the tangent there is horizontal. The formula also shows the method's honest limit: as y approaches 0 the slope grows without bound, which is not a defect but the correct report that the tangent has become vertical, a direction in which no finite slope exists.

questions.explanation: A model answer must identify the failure of the vertical line test as the real obstacle and must then show the chain-rule factor that appears once y is treated as a function of x.
questions.hint: Decide whether y can be written as a single function of x near the top of the circle.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: explain why a variable power calls for logarithmic differentiation
questions.stem: Explain why the power rule cannot be applied directly to x raised to the power x, and what logarithmic differentiation does to get around the problem.

answer.exemplar: The power rule says the derivative of x to the power n is n x to the power n minus 1, and it needs two things that fail at once here: the exponent must be a constant, and the base must be the variable whose derivative is taken. In x to the power x the exponent is itself x, so there is no fixed power to pull down and no fixed number of factors to differentiate. Logarithmic differentiation removes the offending structure rather than fighting it. Take a natural log of both sides, which uses the law of logs to collapse the variable power into a product, giving the logarithm of x to the power x equal to x times the logarithm of x. That right-hand side is a product of two ordinary functions of x, so the sum and product rules apply and it differentiates to the logarithm of x plus 1. To finish, differentiate the log identity itself: the derivative of the log of f is f prime over f, so f prime over f equals the logarithm of x plus 1, and multiplying through by f gives f prime equal to x to the power x times the logarithm of x plus 1. The same two steps, take a log then multiply back at the end, flatten any product or quotient of variable powers such as x squared y cubed, where the ordinary product rule would otherwise demand a separate term for every factor.

questions.explanation: A model answer must state which assumption of the power rule fails and then walk through both halves of the method, since the multiply-back at the end is where marks are usually lost.
questions.hint: Say exactly what the power rule requires of the exponent, then follow the log through and undo it.

questions.learningObjective: state the slope of a parametric curve in terms of the parameter
questions.stem: A plane curve is described by x written as a function of t and y written as a function of t, and a point on the curve is wanted. Which expression gives the slope of the curve at the parameter value in question?

Reflection is a good check rather than an argument: a steep line reflects into a shallow one, and a slope of 2 becomes a slope of one half.

questions.learningObjective: define a critical point correctly
questions.stem: Which statement gives a correct definition of a critical point of a function f?

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: reject a behaviour claim that the derivative sign contradicts
questions.practice: checking a claim against a sign
questions.stem: A report states that a function with a positive derivative at every point of an interval must be falling over that whole interval. How should the report be read?

options.text: the report is false, because a positive derivative means the function rises across the interval
the report is false, but only where the second derivative is also positive
options.misconception: makes the direction of travel depend on the second derivative

options.text: the report is true wherever the second derivative happens to be positive
options.misconception: invokes concavity as the determinant of increase or decrease

options.text: the report cannot be checked without evaluating the function at several points
options.misconception: believes a sign of the derivative cannot settle the direction of travel

questions.explanation: The sign of the first derivative is exactly the statement about direction of travel: positive means the function is increasing, negative means decreasing, and zero means momentarily level. Concavity, which the second derivative measures, says how the slope is changing and has nothing to do with whether the curve is going up or down. Option D mistakes a sign for a sample, and evaluating the function at scattered points can never settle the question as reliably as the sign already does.
questions.hint: The first derivative's sign is the direct statement about direction; the second describes the bend.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: differentiate an inverse function from the original derivative
questions.stem: Let f of x equal x squared for x greater than 0, so an inverse exists. What is the value of the derivative of f inverse at the input where its output is 16?
questions.explanation: The input that produces 16 satisfies x squared = 16 with x positive, so x = 4, and the derivative there is 2x = 8. The derivative of the inverse at that point is the reciprocal, 1/8 = 0.125. The same figure comes from writing the inverse directly as the square root of its input, whose derivative is 1 over 2 times the square root, and at 16 that is 1 over 8 as well.
questions.hint: Find the input that maps to 16, take the reciprocal of f prime there.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: compute a slope from a parametric description
questions.stem: A curve is traced by x equal to 2t plus 3 and y equal to t squared minus 5t. At the parameter value t equal to 4, what is the slope of the curve?
questions.explanation: Differentiating each coordinate with respect to t gives 2 and 2t - 5, so at t = 4 the slope is (8 - 5) over 2 = 3/2 = 1.5. The point itself is (11, -4), since 4 squared minus 20 is -4, and a finite difference of y against x straddling that point returns 1.5 as well. Eliminating the parameter gives the Cartesian curve y = (x squared - 16x + 39) over 4, whose derivative is (x - 8) over 2, and at x = 11 that is again 3/2.
questions.hint: Take the derivative of each coordinate with respect to t, then divide.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: locate a local minimum and evaluate the function there
questions.practice: finding and evaluating a local minimum
questions.stem: The function f of x equal to 2x cubed minus 3x squared minus 12x plus 1 has a local minimum. What is the value of f at that point?
questions.explanation: Differentiating gives 6x squared - 6x - 12, which factors as 6 times (x + 1)(x - 2), so the critical points are x = -1 and x = 2. The derivative is positive just below -1 and negative just above it, so x = -1 is a local maximum, while at x = 2 the derivative goes from negative to positive, making it the local minimum. Substituting gives 2(8) - 3(4) - 24 + 1 = 16 - 12 - 24 + 1 = -19.
questions.hint: Factor the derivative, then use the sign change on each side of each root.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: identify the vertical and horizontal asymptotes of a rational function
questions.stem: The function f of x equals the fraction with numerator 2x plus 1 and denominator x minus 3 has a vertical asymptote and a horizontal asymptote. What is the sum of the x-coordinate of the vertical one and the y-value of the horizontal one?
questions.explanation: The denominator vanishes at x = 3 while the numerator there is 7, which is not 0, so the graph blows up there and x = 3 is the vertical asymptote. The degrees of numerator and denominator are equal, so the graph approaches the ratio of the leading coefficients, 2 over 1 = 2, making y = 2 the horizontal asymptote, and evaluating the fraction at a very large input returns 2. Adding the two readings gives 3 + 2 = 5.
questions.hint: A vertical asymptote comes from a vanishing denominator; a horizontal one from the leading terms.

questions.learningObjective: compare a local maximum with the absolute maximum on a closed interval
questions.stem: On the closed interval that runs from -1 to 3, the function f of x equal to x cubed minus 3x has a local maximum. What is the value of the absolute maximum of f on that interval?
questions.explanation: The derivative 3x squared - 3 vanishes at x = -1 and x = 1, so the candidates on the closed interval are -1, 1, and the endpoints -1 and 3. Their values are 2, -2, and 18, and the largest is 18 at x = 3. The local maximum of 2 at x = -1 is beaten comfortably, which is the point of the item: a local maximum is best only in its own neighbourhood and says nothing about the rest of the domain.

questions.learningObjective: find the intervals on which a function increases
questions.stem: On the closed interval that runs from 0 to 4, the function f of x equal to 3x squared minus 6x is increasing on one sub-interval. What is the length of that sub-interval?
questions.explanation: The derivative is 6x - 6, which is negative for x below 1 and positive for x above 1, so the function falls on the interval from 0 to 1 and rises on the interval from 1 to 4. The increasing stretch therefore has length 4 - 1 = 3. The critical point splits the interval in two, and the sign of the derivative on each side is what says which stretch rises, so both steps are needed.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a limit containing a root by rationalising
questions.stem: What is the limit as x approaches 4 of the fraction with numerator the square root of x plus 5 minus 3 and denominator x minus 4? Give the answer to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: Direct substitution gives 3 minus 3 over 0, which is an undefined form rather than a value, so the numerator has to be rationalised. Multiplying by the conjugate of the radical turns x + 5 - 9 into x - 4, and that cancels the denominator, leaving the limit equal to 1 over the square root of x plus 5 plus 3. At x = 4 that is 1 over 3 plus 3, so 1/6, which is 0.167 to three decimal places.
questions.hint: Multiply by the conjugate of the radical and the x - 4 factor will cancel.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: use a half-angle identity to simplify a derivative
questions.stem: The function f of x equal to the fraction with numerator 1 plus cosine of x and denominator sine of x is hard to differentiate as written. Which simplified expression gives its derivative?

options.text: negative 1 over 2 times the sine squared of x over 2
negative 1 over 2 times the cosine squared of x over 2
options.misconception: swaps sine for cosine while differentiating the half-angle form

options.text: positive 1 over 2 times the sine squared of x over 2
options.misconception: loses the sign that comes from differentiating the cotangent

options.text: negative sine of x over the cosine squared of x
options.misconception: produces the derivative of the secant instead of this function

questions.explanation: The half-angle identity 1 + cosine of x = 2 times the cosine squared of x over 2 turns the function into the cotangent of x over 2, whose derivative is the negative cosecant squared of x over 2 times the inner derivative one half. So the answer is negative 1 over twice the sine squared of x over 2. The quotient rule confirms it independently, giving negative 1 plus cosine of x over the sine squared of x, and the two forms are equal wherever both are defined.
questions.hint: Rewrite the function with a half-angle identity, then differentiate the cotangent.

questions.topic: End behaviour of a rational function
questions.learningObjective: predict the end behaviour of a rational function from its degrees
questions.stem: What happens to the function f of x equal to the fraction with numerator 3x squared plus 1 and denominator x squared minus 4 as x grows without bound in either direction?

options.text: it approaches 3, since equal degrees give the ratio of the leading coefficients
it grows without bound, since the numerator carries the larger constant term
options.misconception: reads a small numerator constant as if it dominated the leading term

options.text: it approaches 0, since the denominator contains a squared term
options.misconception: counts powers inside a term instead of comparing degrees of numerator and denominator

options.text: it falls without bound, since the denominator turns negative past x = 2
options.misconception: lets a sign change near the finite hole dictate behaviour at infinity

questions.explanation: Numerator and denominator have the same degree, so the quotient of the leading coefficients is the limiting value, 3 over 1 = 3, at both ends. The lower-order terms wash out, so the 1 and the -4 make no difference to the limit even though they decide where the graph has its two vertical asymptotes at x = 2 and x = -2. Evaluating at a very large input returns 3 from the positive side and also 3 from the negative side, which rules out option D.
questions.hint: Compare the degrees first, then take the ratio of the leading coefficients.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: maximise an area subject to a perimeter constraint
questions.stem: A farmer encloses a rectangular field against a straight river, so only three sides need fencing. With 200 metres of fencing available for those three sides, what is the largest area in square metres that can be enclosed?

options.text: 5000 square metres
2500 square metres
options.misconception: reports the area of a square built from half the fencing

options.text: 10000 square metres
options.misconception: treats all 200 metres as if they enclosed a full square

options.text: 4000 square metres
options.misconception: squares the width alone and drops the length term entirely

questions.explanation: Letting w be the width, which is fenced on two sides, and L the side along the river, the constraint is 2w + L = 200, so the area is w times 200 minus 2w, that is 200w - 2w squared. Its derivative is 200 - 4w, which vanishes at w = 50, and the second derivative is negative, so that is the maximum. With w = 50 the fenced length is 100 and the area is 50 times 100 = 5000 square metres, and nearby widths such as 49 or 51 give 4998, confirming the peak.
questions.hint: Write the area as a function of one dimension using the fencing constraint, then maximise it.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: correct a monotonicity claim that the derivative sign refutes
questions.stem: For the function f of x equal to x cubed minus 3x, a student reports that f is increasing on the open interval that runs from -1 to 1. What is correct?

options.text: f prime is negative all the way across that interval, so f is decreasing there
the claim holds, because the critical points at the two ends bound the interval
options.misconception: believes critical points delimit the stretch where the function rises

options.text: the claim holds wherever the second derivative stays positive
options.misconception: lets concavity decide the direction of travel

options.text: the claim cannot be judged, since signs of a derivative give no information about increase
options.misconception: denies that a derivative sign settles a question about direction

questions.explanation: The derivative is 3x squared - 3, which is negative for every x strictly between -1 and 1, since 3(x - 1)(x + 1) has opposite signs there. A negative derivative means the function falls as x grows, so the correct reading is decreasing, and the student's claim has the sign backwards. Checking the endpoints is what makes the mistake plausible, since f prime does vanish at both of them, but the behaviour strictly between them is the opposite of what was reported.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: correct a limit declared nonexistent from an undefined form
questions.stem: A student substitutes x equals 0 into the limit of sine of 2x over x, obtains 0 over 0, and concludes that the limit does not exist. What is correct?

options.text: the limit is 2, after rewriting the quotient as 2 times the ratio of sine of 2x to 2x
the limit is 0, since the numerator vanishes as x approaches 0
options.misconception: reads the vanishing numerator as if it fixed the limit by itself

options.text: the limit does not exist, since direct substitution produced an undefined form
options.misconception: confuses the value of a quotient at a point with the limit of that quotient

options.text: the limit is 1, since a function divided by its own input always tends to 1
options.misconception: applies a false general rule instead of the standard trig limit

questions.explanation: The form 0 over 0 is a signal to rewrite, not a verdict, and the rewrite here is to factor 2 out of the sine: sine of 2x over x = 2 times the ratio of sine of 2x to 2x. As x approaches 0 so does 2x, and the standard limit of the sine of an angle over that angle is 1, so the answer is 2. Option C is the misconception the item targets, since a limit describes the approach to a point rather than the value at it, and the function is not even defined at 0.
questions.hint: Rescale the angle so the standard limit of sine over its argument applies.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: explain with an example how a local maximum can fail to be absolute
questions.stem: Explain, using a concrete example, how a local maximum can fail to be an absolute maximum.

answer.exemplar: Local and absolute are statements about different sets of competitors: local compares a point only with the points near it, while absolute compares it with every point in the domain, and nothing forces the neighbourhood to contain the global winner. Take the function f of x equal to x cubed minus 3x on the closed interval from -1 to 3. Its derivative is 3x squared minus 3, which is positive for x below -1 and above 2 and negative in between, so the function climbs to a local maximum at x = -1, where the value is -1 cubed plus 3, that is 2. It then falls to a local minimum of -2 at x = 1, and finally climbs again all the way to the right endpoint, where the value is 27 minus 9, that is 18. The local maximum of 2 is therefore not the absolute maximum, since 18 beats it, even though nothing near x = -1 comes close. The general mechanism is the same in every case: a local maximum is where the derivative changes from positive to negative, which only says the curve turns over locally, and a later stretch of rising curve can still climb past that height.

questions.explanation: A model answer must show a worked example with both values, since the point is the numerical comparison between the local and the absolute winner, and it should say why the local test cannot detect the later climb.
questions.hint: Pick a function on a closed interval, find both its local maximum and its endpoint values, and compare.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: locate a critical point and evaluate the function there
questions.stem: The function f of x equal to 3x squared minus 6x has exactly one critical point. First find its x-coordinate, then find the value of f at that point, and report the second value.

options.text: minus 3
minus 6
options.misconception: reports the linear part of the function and drops the quadratic term

options.text: plus 3
options.misconception: loses a sign while subtracting at the critical point

options.text: minus 1
options.misconception: reports the first stage instead of evaluating the function there

questions.explanation: The derivative is 6x - 6, which vanishes at x = 1, and that is the only critical point since the derivative exists everywhere. Substituting gives f of 1 = 3 - 6 = -3 as the second stage, and the second derivative is the positive constant 6, so the point is indeed a minimum. The value -3 rather than 6 comes from the constant multiple of x dropping out of the derivative while remaining in the function itself, which is exactly the sort of slip the two stages are there to catch.
questions.hint: Set the derivative to zero, then put that input back into the original function.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: differentiate a compound-interest model for an instantaneous rate
questions.stem: An investment grows according to A of t equal to 4000 times e to the power 0.05 t, with t in years. First find the balance at t equal to 3, then find the instantaneous rate of growth at that moment in dollars per year, and report the second value.

options.text: 232.37 dollars per year
4647.34 dollars per year
options.misconception: reports the first stage, the balance, as though it were a rate

options.text: 200.00 dollars per year
options.misconception: keeps only the initial balance times the rate without the growth factor

options.text: 4000.00 dollars per year
options.misconception: drops the exponent entirely and returns the starting balance

questions.explanation: The balance at three years is 4000 times e to the power 0.15, which is 4647.34 as the first stage. Differentiating gives 200 times e to the power 0.05 t, because the 0.05 in the exponent supplies a second factor, and at t = 3 that is 232.37 dollars per year as the second stage. The same figure comes from multiplying the balance by the rate 0.05, since a continuous-growth model always grows at that fixed fraction of the current balance, so 0.05 times 4647.34 is 232.37 as well.
questions.hint: Evaluate the model first, then differentiate it and evaluate once more.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: identify which relation to differentiate in a related-rates problem
questions.stem: A ladder of fixed length leans against a wall with its foot sliding along the floor. What must be differentiated to find how fast the top of the ladder is descending?

options.text: the relation linking the two distances, x squared plus y squared equal to the constant length squared
the height of the ladder, since that is the only quantity that actually changes
options.misconception: differentiates a quantity that is held fixed by the problem

options.text: the length of the ladder, since it must shorten as the foot slides outward
options.misconception: assumes the rigid ladder changes length as it slides

options.text: the angle the ladder makes with the floor, treated as the constant quantity
options.misconception: treats the angle as fixed, which is the whole point of the problem

questions.explanation: The two distances are tied together by the fixed length, so the relation x squared plus y squared equal to the length squared is the one that holds at every instant and can therefore be differentiated in time. Differentiating it gives 2x times the rate of x plus 2y times the rate of y equals 0, which links the two rates. The ladder's length and the angle are both constant, so neither has a rate to report, and the whole method depends on writing down the constraint before looking for any derivative.
questions.hint: Find the equation that stays true at every moment, then differentiate that with respect to time.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: predict a polynomial's end behaviour from its degree and leading coefficient
questions.stem: A polynomial has degree 4 and a negative leading coefficient. What does its graph do at the two ends?

options.text: it falls to the left and falls to the right
it rises to the left and falls to the right
options.misconception: applies the odd-degree pattern while ignoring the sign of the leading term

options.text: it rises to the left and rises to the right
options.misconception: knows even degrees rise at both ends but misses the negative sign

options.text: it falls to the left and rises to the right
options.misconception: takes the negative sign to apply to only one end of the graph

questions.explanation: For a polynomial the leading term dominates once x is large, so a degree-4 term behaves like a constant multiple of x to the fourth power, and that power is positive however large x is in either direction. A negative coefficient then makes both ends fall, and the lower-degree terms cannot change that for large enough x. The sign of the leading coefficient always applies to both ends together, which is what rules out the last option.
questions.hint: The leading term decides both ends, and an even power has the same sign at both.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: apply the second derivative test when the second derivative is positive
questions.stem: At a critical point of a function the derivative is zero and the second derivative turns out to be positive. What does the second derivative test say about that point?

options.text: it is a local minimum, since the curve is bending upward there
it is a local maximum, since the curve stops falling there
options.misconception: reads a positive curvature as though it meant a peak

options.text: it is an inflection point, since a positive second derivative means a bend
options.misconception: treats any nonzero curvature as a change of concavity

options.text: the test is inconclusive, because only a zero second derivative is decisive
options.misconception: reverses the test, treating a zero rather than a nonzero value as informative

That is exactly a local minimum, and the same reasoning with a negative second derivative gives a local maximum. The inconclusive case is the zero value, where the slope could be rising throughout, falling throughout, or rising then falling, and only the first-derivative test separates those.
questions.hint: Ask whether the slope is increasing or decreasing as the curve passes through the point.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: state when a limit may be evaluated by substitution
questions.stem: When is it legitimate to evaluate a limit simply by putting the target value into the function?

options.text: when the function is defined and continuous at that point, so no undefined form appears
always, since a limit is nothing more than a value read off the function
options.misconception: equates a limit with the function's value at the point, which can differ

options.text: only when the function is a polynomial, since no other expression is continuous
options.misconception: believes continuity is confined to polynomials and rules out roots and logs

options.text: only when the target value is not a zero of any denominator present
options.misconception: makes denominator zeros the only possible obstruction and misses removable holes

questions.explanation: A limit describes the value the function approaches, and when the function is actually defined at the point its value is that limiting value, so substitution is exact rather than approximate. Option C is far too narrow, since square roots, exponentials, and logarithms are all continuous on their domains and substitute perfectly well.

questions.learningObjective: state the limit that defines a derivative
questions.stem: Which of these four expressions is the limit that defines the derivative of a function f at a point a?

options.text: as h approaches 0 of the fraction with numerator f of a plus h minus f of a and denominator h
as h approaches 0 of the fraction with numerator f of a plus h and denominator h
options.misconception: omits the subtraction of the function's value at the point

options.text: as h approaches 0 of the fraction with numerator f of h minus f of a and denominator h
options.misconception: varies the point instead of the step, so the point drifts as h shrinks

options.misconception: reverses the subtraction and so measures a fall instead of a rise

The point a stays fixed while h shrinks, which is why option C, with h inside the function, is a different limit altogether. Keeping a fixed and letting the step shrink is the feature that makes the limit equal the instantaneous rate rather than an average over a distance.

questions.stem: The function g of x equal to the natural logarithm of the quantity 3x plus 1 is a logarithm of an inner expression. Which expression gives its derivative?

questions.stem: A ladder 13 units long leans against a wall, and its foot slides away from the wall at 2 units per second. At the moment the foot is 5 units from the wall, at what rate is the top sliding down, in units per second?

The size of the change is the point: the fifth-degree term dominates by thousands, which is what the degree and sign of the leading coefficient predict.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: find where a function is concave up on a closed interval
questions.stem: The function f of x equal to 3x cubed minus 12x squared has a second derivative of 18x minus 24. Over the interval from 0 to 3, what is the length of the stretch on which the graph is concave up?
questions.explanation: Concavity up is where the second derivative is positive, and 18x - 24 vanishes at x equal to 24 over 18, which is 4/3. The second derivative is negative below that and positive above it, so within the interval from 0 to 3 the concave-up stretch runs from 4/3 to 3, a length of 3 - 4/3 = 5/3, about 1.67. The point 4/3 is where the concavity changes, since the sign flips there, and that is what separates the two stretches.
questions.hint: Solve 18x minus 24 for zero, then measure from there to the right endpoint.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a limit by substituting where the function is defined
questions.stem: What is the limit as x approaches 2 of the fraction with numerator 3x minus 1 and denominator x squared plus 4?
questions.explanation: The denominator at x = 2 is 4 + 4 = 8, which is not zero, so the function is defined there and the limit is simply the value: 6 - 1 over 8, that is 5/8 or 0.625. As a check, rewriting the pieces around x = 2 gives 3(x - 2) + 5 in the numerator and (x - 2)(x + 2) + 8 in the denominator, and the leftover (x - 2) terms vanish as x approaches 2, leaving 5 over 8 once more. Nothing needs cancelling here, which is what distinguishes this case from a factorisation limit.
questions.hint: Check whether the denominator vanishes at the target value; if not, substitute directly.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a difference quotient limit by factorising
questions.stem: What is the limit as h approaches 0 of the fraction with numerator the quantity h plus 4 squared minus 16 and denominator h?
questions.explanation: Expanding the numerator gives h squared plus 8h plus 16 minus 16, which is h squared plus 8h, and that factors as h times the quantity h plus 8. Cancelling the h against the denominator leaves h + 8, whose limit as h approaches 0 is 8. The quotient is undefined at h = 0 itself, which is precisely why the question is phrased as a limit, and taking a small nonzero step confirms the same value.
questions.hint: Expand the square, then factor out the h before letting it go to zero.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: differentiate a quotient of linear expressions
questions.stem: For the function f of x equal to the fraction with numerator 2x plus 1 and denominator x minus 3, what is the value of f prime at the point where x equals 4?
questions.explanation: The quotient rule gives the numerator's derivative times the denominator minus the numerator times the denominator's derivative, all over the denominator squared. That is 2(x - 3) - (2x + 1) over (x - 3) squared, and the x terms cancel to leave minus 7 over (x - 3) squared. At x = 4 the squared term is 1, so the value is -7, and a numerical difference quotient at that point returns the same figure.
questions.hint: Apply the quotient rule, then simplify before substituting.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: differentiate an exponential with a constant multiple of the variable
questions.stem: For the function f of x equal to 3 times e to the power 2x, what is the value of f prime at the point where x equals 1? Give the answer to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The exponential is its own derivative, and the chain rule supplies the factor 2 from the exponent, so f prime of x is 3 times 2 times e to the power 2x. At x = 1 that is 6 times e squared, and e squared is about 7.389, giving 44.33. The factor 2 is exactly what a missing chain-rule step would lose, and a numerical difference quotient at 1 agrees with the closed form to five decimal places.
questions.hint: The exponential keeps itself, and the chain rule contributes the 2 from the exponent.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: classify two critical points with the second derivative test
questions.stem: The function f of x equal to 2x cubed minus 9x squared plus 12x has two critical points. What does the second derivative test say about each of them?

options.text: x = 1 is a local maximum and x = 2 is a local minimum
x = 1 is a local minimum and x = 2 is a local maximum
options.misconception: swaps the two classifications by reading the curvature the wrong way round

options.text: both points are local minima, since the derivative vanishes at each of them
options.misconception: treats a vanishing derivative as a minimum regardless of the curvature

options.text: the test is inconclusive at both points, since the second derivative is linear
options.misconception: believes a linear second derivative cannot be read at a fixed point

questions.explanation: The derivative is 6x squared - 18x + 12, which factors as 6 times (x - 1)(x - 2), so the critical points are 1 and 2. The second derivative is 12x - 18, which is -6 at x = 1 and 6 at x = 2, so the first is concave down there and the second concave up. Concave down at a critical point means a peak and concave up means a valley, giving a local maximum at 1 and a local minimum at 2, exactly as the first option states.
questions.hint: Factor the derivative to find the critical points, then read the sign of the second derivative at each.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: solve a related-rates problem for an elliptical constraint
questions.stem: Two points are linked by the relation x squared plus 4y squared equals 25. If x is growing at 3 units per second, how fast is y changing at the moment when x equals 3?

options.text: y is falling at 1.125 units per second
y is falling at 0.375 units per second
options.misconception: reports dy over dx and forgets to multiply by the rate of x

options.text: y is rising at 1.125 units per second
options.misconception: loses the sign when solving for the rate of y

options.text: y is falling at 2.250 units per second
options.misconception: doubles the answer by counting the 4 in the relation twice

questions.explanation: At x = 3 the relation gives 9 + 4y squared = 25, so y squared = 4 and y = 2. Differentiating with respect to time gives 2x times the rate of x plus 8y times the rate of y equal to 0, so the rate of y is minus 18 over 16, which is -1.125. Writing y as one half of the square root of 25 minus x squared and differentiating that directly gives -0.375 for the slope against x, and multiplying by the rate of 3 returns the same -1.125.
questions.hint: Find y at that moment first, then differentiate the relation in time and solve.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: correct a related-rates equation missing a time derivative
questions.stem: A student differentiates the ladder relation x squared plus y squared equal to 13 squared and writes down 2x times the rate of x equals 2y, then solves that for the rate of y. What is the flaw?

options.text: the rate of y was never introduced, because differentiating in time gives 2x times the rate of x plus 2y times the rate of y equal to 0
the length of the ladder must be differentiated too, since it changes as the foot moves
options.misconception: believes the rigid length varies and must appear on the right-hand side

options.text: the square of 13 was dropped, so the right-hand side should be 13 rather than 169
options.misconception: argues about a constant term that differentiation would never touch

options.text: the chain rule was not applied to the constant 169 on the right-hand side
options.misconception: expects a time derivative from a quantity that does not vary with time

questions.explanation: Both x and y are functions of time, so differentiating the relation produces a term for each, giving 2x times the rate of x plus 2y times the rate of y equal to 0 because the right-hand side is constant. The student's equation omits the second term entirely, which is what makes it impossible to solve for the rate of y, since the remaining equation has no unknown rate in it. The other three options all chase a right-hand side that carries no time dependence, and differentiating a constant would give zero anyway.
questions.hint: Count how many quantities in the relation depend on time; each contributes one term.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: correct an end-behaviour claim based on degree alone
questions.practice: catching a sign error in end behaviour
questions.stem: A student says that every polynomial of odd degree must fall as x grows without bound. What is correct?

options.text: the claim is false, because the sign of the leading coefficient decides, and a positive one rises at the right end
the claim is true, since an odd power is negative for a negative input
options.misconception: reads a property of the left end as if it settled the right end too

options.text: the claim is true, and an odd degree always produces a horizontal asymptote
options.misconception: attaches an asymptote to a function that grows without bound

options.text: the claim cannot be judged without knowing the constant term of the polynomial
options.misconception: believes the constant term controls what happens far from the origin

questions.explanation: The degree fixes the parity, so an odd degree does guarantee opposite ends, but the sign of the leading coefficient fixes which end rises. For the polynomial 2x to the fifth minus 7x cubed plus x the leading coefficient is positive, so the graph rises to the right and falls to the left, which is the opposite of what the student asserted. A polynomial grows without bound at both ends, so it has no horizontal asymptote, and the constant term has no say in behaviour far from the origin.
questions.hint: The degree gives opposite ends; the sign of the leading term gives the direction.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: explain how the sign of a derivative settles increase and decrease
questions.stem: Explain how the sign of the first derivative settles whether a function is increasing, decreasing, or level on an interval.

answer.exemplar: The derivative at a point is a limit of difference quotients, and each quotient is a rise over a run taken with the run positive, so its sign is the sign of the rise when the step is made small. A positive derivative therefore means every sufficiently small step to the right gains height, and a negative derivative means the same step loses height, while a zero derivative means the height is momentarily unchanged. Carrying that local statement across a whole interval needs one extra step, because a positive derivative at one point says nothing about the point beside it. What makes the statement valid over an interval is that a derivative which is positive at every point of the interval makes the average rate of change over any stretch of that interval positive, and a positive average rate means the net change is positive. That is also the reason a single vanishing derivative is not enough to declare a maximum, since the sign may not change at all. Finally, if the derivative fails to exist at one interior point, as it does at a corner or a cusp, the interval must be split there and each piece handled on its own, since the direction of travel can change exactly at the break.

questions.explanation: A model answer must connect the difference quotient to the sign of the rise and then supply the argument that carries the local statement to a whole interval, since that gap is where most wrong explanations fail.
questions.hint: Start from what a difference quotient measures, then address why the local statement extends to an interval.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: locate a change in concavity and evaluate the function there
questions.stem: Take the function f of x equal to x cubed minus 3x squared. First find the x-coordinate where its concavity changes, then find the value of f at that point, and report the second value.

options.text: minus 2
plus 2
options.misconception: loses a sign while evaluating at the inflection point

options.text: minus 1
options.misconception: reports the first stage instead of evaluating the function there

options.text: minus 6
options.misconception: uses twice the x-coordinate instead of the function's value

questions.explanation: The second derivative is 6x - 6, which vanishes at x = 1, and it is negative just below that and positive just above, so the concavity really does change there and x = 1 is a genuine inflection point. Substituting gives 1 - 3 = -2 as the second stage. The vanishing second derivative alone would not have been enough, since a point can be flat with the curvature on the same side, which is why the sign check is part of the first stage.
questions.hint: Solve the second derivative for zero, verify the sign changes, then evaluate the function.
